title: The pharmacokinetics of an I V infusion

segs.text: Module three, objective one. What happens to a drug given by I V infusion. An intravenous infusion runs drug into a vein at a constant rate for a set time, instead of giving it all at once as an I V bolus. The infusion rate, R, is the amount of drug put in per unit of time, most often milligrams per hour. A constant rate in is a zero order input, because it stays the same whatever the concentration. Elimination stays first order, exactly as after a bolus: a fixed fraction of the drug present leaves each hour, and that fraction is the elimination rate constant, k.

card.m: infusion: constant rate, set time; bolus: all at once
R: amount per time, mg/hr
input: zero order, R constant
elimination: first order; k = fraction leaving per hour, hr<sup>−1</sup>

segs.text: She said, the only thing that's changing here is the input. At the start no drug is in the body, so C p, the plasma concentration, is zero and almost nothing leaves. The amount leaving each hour is k times the amount in the body, so it grows as drug builds up. While R is larger than the amount leaving each hour, drug accumulates and C p rises. The rise slows as the amount leaving each hour approaches R, and when the two are equal the level stops changing: this plateau is steady state, and its level is C s s, the steady state concentration.

card.m: start: C<sub>p</sub> = 0, almost nothing leaves
amount out per hour = k × amount in the body: grows as C<sub>p</sub> grows
R > amount out per hour → C<sub>p</sub> rises
R = amount out per hour → plateau, C<sub>ss</sub>

segs.text: Her opening poll for this module asked what rises when an I V bolus dose is raised. Only the concentration does; the clearance, the volume of plasma emptied of drug each hour, the half-life and the apparent volume of distribution stay the same, because they describe how this patient handles the drug, not how much was given. The same holds for an infusion: a higher R gives higher concentrations, and at the plateau the amount eliminated each hour equals the new R. k and the clearance do not change with R.

card.m: her poll: bolus dose raised → what rises?
C<sub>p</sub> rises; Cl, t<sub>½</sub>, V<sub>D</sub> unchanged
textbook: R 30 → 40 mg/hr; amount out per hour at the plateau 30 → 40 mg/hr
k, Cl: unchanged by R

segs.text: Cessation means stopping the infusion. After it nothing comes in, so C p falls by first order elimination alone, the same fall as after a bolus. The fraction lost each hour is still k, so on a log plot the fall has the same slope whether the infusion stopped at steady state or before it. She said, Our input is zero order, constant in, first order out. When we stop the in, then it's just out.

card.m: after cessation: no input, first order fall
stopped at or before steady state: same k, same slope
zero order in, first order out; stop → only out

segs.text: Why infuse at all? A constant input gives precise control of C p, and the textbook adds that for a drug with a narrow therapeutic window, such as heparin, it avoids wide swings between the highest and lowest levels. With R, k and the volume or the clearance known, C p can be predicted at any time during or after the infusion, and every calculation in this module does that.

card.m: infusion: precise control of C<sub>p</sub>
narrow window, e.g. heparin: no wide peak and trough swings
R, k, V<sub>D</sub> or Cl → C<sub>p</sub> at any time

segs.text: Her practice problem asks for the rate of an infusion in two forms. Two hundred milligrams of an analgesic are dissolved in five hundred milliliters of five percent dextrose and run over twenty four hours. R is an amount per time, so it is the amount infused divided by the time it runs: eight point three three milligrams per hour. A pump is set in volume per time, so the same division uses the five hundred milliliters instead, and the hours are converted to minutes. The result, zero point three five milliliters per minute, is the same infusion described by the volume of solution instead of the amount of drug.

card.m: 200 mg in 500 mL, over 24 hr
R = {{frac:amount|time}}
{{frac:500 mL|24 hr}} = 20.83 mL/hr
{{frac:500 mL|24 hr}} × {{frac:1 hr|60 min}} = 0.347 mL/min
0.35 mL/min

segs.text: Three rates in this module have three different units, and mixing them up is the common error. R is how much drug goes in each hour, in milligrams per hour; k is what fraction of the drug present leaves each hour, in per hour; and the clearance is how many liters of plasma are emptied of drug each hour, in liters per hour. A zero order input does not make a zero order drug: in her review poll the infusion was the zero order input, and elimination was first order after a bolus, an oral dose and an infusion alike. The words constant rate or continuous infusion signal this pattern.

card.m: R: amount per time, mg/hr
k: fraction per time, hr<sup>−1</sup>
Cl: volume per time, L/hr
bolus: all at once in; oral: first order in; infusion: zero order in
all three: first order out
constant rate, continuous infusion → zero order in, first order out

segs.text: Her stems also need unit work first. V D, the apparent volume of distribution, is the volume that relates the amount of drug in the body to C p, and it may be given per kilogram. In her solution one hundred ten pounds became fifty kilograms, since one kilogram is two point two pounds, and three liters per kilogram then became one hundred fifty liters. Objective two explains the plateau, objective seven the fall after stopping, and objectives four and five add a loading dose so the patient does not wait for the climb.

card.m: V<sub>D</sub>: links the amount in the body to C<sub>p</sub>; may be L/kg
{{frac:110 lb|2.2 lb/kg}} = 50 kg
VD = 3 L/kg × 50 kg = 150 L
→ plateau (obj. 2), fall after stopping (obj. 7), loading dose (obj. 4, 5)
